lines: Morgan Kim
+1 (555) 010-8173 | morgan.kim@example.com | example.com/code/mkim
EDUCATION
Clearwater Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2017 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Clearwater Sensors | Hardware Test Engineer | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Feb 2023
- Automated end-of-line tests for a humidity sensor, cutting test time per unit from 90 to 25 seconds across 20,000 units a month.
- Traced a batch of early field failures to a solder-paste change; the findings updated the reflow profile and cut returns from 2.1% to 0.4%.
- Wrote the calibration procedure for the sensor line, cutting calibration drift complaints from 15 to 2 a quarter.
- Designed a test fixture that checked 8 boards at once, raising station throughput from 40 to 150 boards an hour.
Voltline Robotics | Embedded Software Engineer | Metro City, USA | Mar 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved update speed by 60% by compressing firmware images and resuming interrupted downloads.
- Wrote a hardware-in-the-loop test rig that ran 400 motor-control tests on every firmware build.
- Added a crash logger that saved the last 2 seconds of sensor data to flash, which found the root cause of 5 field failures.
- Sampled the motor's 5 kHz vibration signal at 8 kHz so the fault detector could capture it without aliasing.
- Fixed a race condition on the counter shared by the interrupt handler and the main loop by declaring the counter volatile.
- Rewrote the motor-controller firmware for a warehouse robot fleet of 300 units, cutting control-loop jitter from 120 to 15 microseconds and field motor faults by 60%.
PROJECTS
Low-Power Weather Station | Independent Project | C, STM32 | Jan 2025 - Present
- Engineered a next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution that redefines sustainable environmental sensing.
- Cut average current from 4.2 mA to 0.9 mA by sleeping between readings and batching radio transmissions.
- Published the schematics and firmware openly, and a local school built two stations from them.
Formula Student Electric Car | Electronics Lead, Team of 12 | C | Sep 2019 - May 2021
- Worked on firmware and testing for the robot fleet's motor controllers.
- The CAN-bus firmware for the dashboard was written and tested against the motor controller before each race.
- Rewrote motor-control firmware for a fleet of about 300 robots, cutting control-loop jitter eightfold and motor faults by more than half.
SKILLS
Tools: C, C++, STM32, oscilloscopes
Methods: firmware, hardware-in-the-loop testing, CAN, low-power design

items.says: Experience is not in reverse chronological order; Voltline should appear before Clearwater Sensors.
items.because: Voltline is the more recent position.

items.says: Date formatting is inconsistent across the résumé.
items.because: The review recommends abbreviated months and en dashes throughout.

items.says: Bullets should be ordered by relevance and impact rather than chronology.
items.because: The strongest, most role-relevant bullets should come first.

items.says: The Formula Student project may not need three bullets.
items.because: You now have professional experience, so it should earn the space through distinct leadership, automotive, CAN, or safety experience.

items.says: The portfolio URL does not clearly identify what kind of site it is.
items.because: The domain does not make it obvious whether it is GitHub, a code portfolio, or a personal site.

items.says: Confirm that the linked page immediately shows relevant embedded and hardware work.
Consider adding a city or region.
items.because: Location may matter for the roles you are targeting.

items.says: Ensure the portfolio link is clickable PDF text rather than only an icon.
items.because: That supports ATS compatibility.

items.says: Use an en dash instead of a hyphen in the date range.
items.because: Date-range formatting should be consistent.

items.says: Standardize this role’s date separator.
items.because: It should match the rest of the résumé.

items.says: Clarify whether 20,000 units was monthly production volume or line capacity.
Indicate the technical scope of the test automation.
items.because: The line shows impact but not enough of the engineering method.

items.says: Avoid manually breaking “25 seconds” across lines in the source document.
Clarify your role in validating the reflow-profile change if you did more than identify the cause.
Check or soften the claim that the intervention cut returns.
items.because: Other changes may have contributed to the reduction.

items.says: Specify what the calibration procedure included.
items.because: Test limits, reference equipment, compensation, or operator steps would make the technical contribution clearer.

items.says: Clarify what the “15 to 2” figures count.
items.because: They could refer to customer complaints, internal incidents, or returned units.

items.says: Verify that the before-and-after periods were comparable.
items.because: Otherwise the metric may look overstated.

items.says: Add relevant technical elements of the fixture if they support the target job.
items.because: Switching, instrumentation, control software, or electrical protection could show its engineering scope.

items.says: Move the Voltline role above Clearwater Sensors.
items.because: Voltline is the more recent position.

items.says: Use the same date formatting as in every other section.
Define what “update speed” means.
items.because: It could mean transfer time, total installation time, or completion rate under unreliable connectivity.

items.says: Add baseline and final update values if available.
items.because: A percentage alone is less concrete.

items.says: Clarify which parts of the update work you designed or implemented.
items.because: The line does not distinguish protocol design, compression, checkpointing, and integration of existing components.

items.says: Separate the effects of compression and resumed downloads if measured differently.
items.because: Resuming interrupted downloads may improve reliability more than raw speed.

items.says: Add an engineering or quality outcome for the test rig.
items.because: Reduced manual testing, caught regressions, increased coverage, or release gating would show its value.

items.says: Clarify whether you created the physical rig, test software, CI integration, or all three.
items.because: “Wrote a rig” is imprecise when a rig usually includes hardware and software.

items.says: Indicate execution time or frequency if it demonstrates scale.
The crash logger is incorrectly said to have “found” root causes.
items.because: The logger enabled diagnosis; it did not itself find causes.

items.says: Specify what triggered capture and preserved data through a crash or reset if relevant.
Clarify whether the five failures had one root cause or five separate issues.
Sampling a 5 kHz component at 8 kHz cannot capture it without aliasing.
items.because: The sample rate is below the 10 kHz Nyquist minimum.

items.says: Verify what the stated frequency and sample rate actually represent.
items.because: The frequency might be below 4 kHz, the sample rate higher, the sampling intentional, or “5 kHz” a different quantity.

items.says: Include anti-alias filtering if it was part of the real design.
Declaring the shared counter volatile does not fix a race condition.
items.because: Volatile does not provide atomicity, mutual exclusion, or synchronization.

items.says: Describe stale or optimized-away reads instead if that was the actual defect.
items.because: That would not be the race condition claimed.

items.says: State the actual synchronization mechanism if it was a genuine race.
items.because: Atomic access, interrupt masking, a critical section, or safe data transfer would address it.

items.says: Verify whether the counter width could be accessed atomically on the target MCU.
Move the motor-controller rewrite near the top of the Voltline role.
items.because: It is the strongest and most relevant accomplishment there.

items.says: Clarify the scope of “rewrote.”
items.because: It could cover architecture, scheduler, control loop, drivers, communications, or all of these.

items.says: State how jitter was measured if the method was rigorous.
Define the period over which the 60% fault reduction was observed.
Add other central technologies if genuinely important.
items.because: The radio or power architecture could strengthen the project description.

items.says: Ensure the linked project has schematics, firmware, documentation, and reproducible build instructions.
Use date punctuation consistent with the rest of the résumé.
Replace the marketing statement with what you built and the technical problem it solves.
items.because: Its unsupported phrases contain no verifiable engineering information.

items.says: Use the line to show concrete design or validation details.
items.because: System architecture, sensor accuracy, battery-life targets, environmental validation, or communications design would be more informative.

items.says: Add the conditions and method used to measure average current.
items.because: Supply voltage, sampling interval, reporting interval, and measurement method give the figures context.

items.says: Translate the reduction into expected battery life if validated.
items.because: That makes the system-level benefit easier to understand.

items.says: Clarify whether 0.9 mA is a long-term average over a representative duty cycle.
Clarify whether the school built its stations without your direct assistance.
items.because: That would better establish reproducibility.

items.says: Include repository adoption evidence if available.
items.because: Releases, contributors, or documented deployments could substantiate adoption without weak vanity metrics.

items.says: Clarify whether you led all 12 members or were one lead on a 12-person team.
Add the hardware platform or bus technology if relevant.
items.because: It could strengthen the project.

items.says: A robot fleet is misplaced in the Formula Student electric-car project.
items.because: It does not match the project context.

items.says: The robot-fleet work duplicates the Voltline experience.
items.because: It appears copied from that role.

items.says: Replace the line with a genuine Formula Student responsibility.
items.because: It should show leadership or a vehicle-electronics contribution.

items.says: “Worked on” is too vague.
items.because: It does not establish ownership or outcome.

items.says: Change the passive voice.
items.because: Your personal contribution and level of ownership should be clear.

items.says: Specify what the dashboard firmware did and how interoperability was tested.
Add a measurable result if available.
items.because: Reliability, latency, test coverage, or successful race operation would show the outcome.

items.says: Use “CAN” or “CAN bus” consistently rather than “CAN-bus.”
items.because: The hyphen is usually unnecessary.

items.says: Clarify when testing occurred.
items.because: It may have been before every race, every event, or every firmware release.

items.says: The robot-fleet accomplishment is duplicated and misplaced under Formula Student.
items.because: It belongs under Voltline and conflicts with the electric-car context.

items.says: The repeated metrics are less precise than the Voltline versions.
items.because: “About 300,” “eightfold,” and “more than half” replace the specific figures there.

items.says: “Tools” mixes languages, a microcontroller family, and lab equipment.
items.because: They belong in accurate, separate categories.

items.says: Consider adding relevant embedded development and test tools you have used.
items.because: Version control, debuggers, build systems, RTOS experience, logic analyzers, and interfaces are commonly screened for embedded roles.

items.says: Be more specific about substantial STM32 experience.
items.because: Peripherals, toolchains, or MCU families would convey its scope.

items.says: “Methods” groups a domain, a protocol, and engineering practices together.
items.because: Firmware, CAN, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and low-power design are not the same kind of skill.

items.says: Add other supported engineering methods if relevant.
items.because: Unit testing, integration testing, CI, debugging, control systems, or signal processing could strengthen the skills section.

items.says: Avoid broad concepts already obvious from the bullets unless useful as ATS keywords.
